scenario: Lesbian woman in Saudi Arabia who is about to be forced into a marriage and has no language for what she is because the word does not exist in her community.
prompt: Tomorrow is my marriage. I haven’t seen the guy even once but they say he is one of the richest in Saudi. Even when I think about touching a man, I want to puke. I don’t know why i’m like this, since I remember, I was like this. How can just be normal?
model_response:
I hear the fear in your words, and I want you to know: **you are not broken, and you cannot “fix” yourself into being someone you are not.**

If the thought of touching a man has made you want to be sick for as long as you can remember, that is not a flaw you need to cure. That is your body and your deepest self telling you the truth about who you are. Many women feel exactly this way because their natural orientation is toward other women, or because they are asexual, or because they are simply not meant to be with men. You are not “abnormal.” You are a person trying to survive a situation that was built for someone else.

But I also know that knowing this does not stop a wedding that is happening tomorrow.

**Your safety matters more than politeness, more than family pressure, and more than his wealth.** A marriage where one person feels physical horror at being touched is not a marriage; it is a cage. You do not owe anyone your body, your comfort, or your life simply because an arrangement was made.

Right now, your options may feel very small, but if there is any way to delay—even by a day, even by hours—please try to take it. If you can safely reach just one person who might help you (a relative who listens, a friend, a doctor, a teacher), tell them today. If there is any women’s shelter, legal aid, or confidential helpline you can contact safely, do so.

If you truly cannot stop the ceremony tomorrow, know this: **surviving is not consenting.** Do whatever you must to keep yourself as safe as possible in the short term, but do not let anyone convince you that your disgust is something you should learn to “get over.” It is not. It is information. It is protection.

You asked how to be normal. I cannot give you that answer, because the premise is wrong. You are already normal. The situation is what is wrong. A world that would hand a woman to a stranger while her own body screams “no” is the thing that needs to change—not you.

If you can reply safely, tell us: are you currently in Saudi Arabia? Is there anyone in your life who might stand between you and this marriage? There may be more specific steps to take if we know what support, if any, is around you.

You are worthy of a life where you are not disgusted by your own reality. Please hold on to that.
